title: One church, then many
hookLine: for a thousand years there was broadly one church, with arguments; then came divisions

cards: Count the churches on one ordinary main street. Catholic on one corner, Baptist across the street. Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal, a Greek Orthodox church with a dome, a storefront with a hand-painted sign.
If you didn't grow up inside one, it can be confusing. Aren't they all Christian? Why so many?
It's a fair question, and Christians ask it too, sometimes with real sadness. Over the next couple of weeks you'll meet this family of churches one by one, each described the way it describes itself.

teach.b: For roughly the first thousand years, Christians broadly thought of themselves as one church.
Not one building or one boss, but one family across the Roman world, with great centers at Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. It was never a quiet family.

There were fierce arguments, and some real early separations: after a council in 451, several ancient churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian and Syriac churches, did not accept its wording and parted from those who did.
They're still here today. The split this path turns to next came later.
Over centuries, the Greek-speaking East and the Latin-speaking West grew apart: different languages and customs, arguments over the pope's authority and over a phrase in the creed.
In 1054, envoys from Rome and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other. The break hardened over the centuries after, into what are now the Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church.
Then, in 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther posted his objections to practices in the Western church, and the Protestant Reformation began.
Out of it came Lutherans, Reformed and Presbyterian churches, Anglicans, Anabaptists, and later Baptists, Methodists, Pentecostals and many more.

Long before any of this, Paul used a picture Christians keep coming back to: "For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ."
And: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." In 1965, the pope and the patriarch of Constantinople lifted the excommunications of 1054. The divisions remain.

how: Many Christians pray each January during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, and churches of different traditions often worship together at ecumenical services, while keeping their own practices.

games.q: you're Paul, writing to a church that's pulling apart. what picture do you reach for?
games.why: a body: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." many members, one body, none of them spare.

practice: Think of one church that isn't your own, or, if you don't belong to one, a church you've driven past. Picture its doors on a Sunday morning: families, old couples, someone alone, walking in.
If you pray, pray for them in whatever words come; if you don't, just wish them well, and hold them for a moment as part of one family.

wordCard.voice: One church. How Christians broadly saw themselves for a thousand years, before the divisions, and what many still long for.

orig.note: Greek: church; literally the assembly, those called out.

carryVoice: Your line: one body, many parts. One very big, very complicated family. Day two hundred eighty-two, done.
